rulings.rationale: The paired genre notices complete a book threshold before the divine-character hymn opens, so the heading remains recoverable without pretending to develop the following oracle.
rulings.counterevidence: The heading frames the whole book and is too brief to interpret independently without its book parent.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Merging 1:1 with 1:2-8 would hide the heading-to-hymn seam and turn framing metadata into the first hymnic predicate.

rulings.rationale: Divine character, cosmic manifestation, human inability to stand, refuge, and enemy pursuit form one coherent hymn whose 1:7-8 contrast functions as its paired climax rather than a detached maxim.
rulings.counterevidence: The renewed good-refuge assertion at 1:7 is a real stanza pressure, and literary and canonical primaries favored a dependent 1:7-8 child.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Splitting 1:2-6 from 1:7-8 would make the positive-negative antithesis look independent of the avenging, slow-to-anger, and theophanic predicates that frame it.

rulings.rationale: Challenge, total-end verdict, consumption imagery, and identification of hostile counsel complete one accusatory address before the Thus-says formula resets the discourse at 1:12.
rulings.counterevidence: The full-end phrase links backward to 1:8, and feminine address at 1:11 does not resolve the historical identity of the target.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 1:14 would cross the marked 1:11 closure and absorb the paired release-and-doom decree into the plot indictment.

rulings.rationale: Release of the afflicted addressee and extinction of the hostile name are deliberately juxtaposed as a paired reversal inside the section bounded by the samekh after 1:11 and pe after 1:14.
rulings.counterevidence: The gender and addressee shift at 1:14 is genuine; literary and canonical primaries treated the hostile decree as independently recoverable.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Splitting 1:12-13 from 1:14 would honor the renewed formula but weaken the paired oppressor-removal and delivered-community reversal that the paragraph closure holds together.

rulings.rationale: Announcement, named audience, cultic imperatives, and their enemy-removal rationale form a complete herald speech after the pe following WEB and WLC 1:14.
rulings.counterevidence: The verse realizes the preceding hostile termination and forms a contrast with the attacker alarm that follows.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Merging with 1:12-14 would absorb Judah's proclamation into the hostile decree, while merging with 2:1-2 would confuse its audience with the besieged city.

rulings.rationale: Alarm and causal rationale make a concise paired opening: 2:2 explains the literary function of the attack warning and cannot safely become a detached restoration claim.
rulings.counterevidence: The besieged addressee in 2:1 and Jacob-Israel in 2:2 differ, while attacker imagery continues into 2:3.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Absorbing 2:1-2 into the detailed tableau beginning at 2:3 would hide the imperative-and-rationale threshold before shields and chariots take over.

rulings.rationale: Military preparation, assault, breach, deportation, flight, plunder, and bodily terror are sequential phases of one accelerating collapse tableau whose outcome is reached at 2:10.
rulings.counterevidence: Nahum 2:7 is syntactically difficult, and 2:8 names Nineveh while shifting to flight and plunder; the Hebrew primary favored two dependent scene children.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Splitting 2:3-7 from 2:8-10 would recognize the move from breach to aftermath, but both children require the same attack-to-desolation action and mandatory whole-scene hydration.

rulings.rationale: The direct first-person verdict extinguishes each element of the lion boast and therefore completes, rather than merely follows, the taunt.
rulings.counterevidence: The renewed direct-divine formula gives 2:13 real standalone pressure inside the larger unit.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Detaching 2:13 would honor its divine-speech formula but sever the verdict from the metaphor and rhetorical question it resolves.

rulings.rationale: The vivid assault register is syntactically and rhetorically completed by its because-clause, so woe, casualties, and charge remain one indictment.
rulings.counterevidence: The cause in 3:4 directly grounds the 3:5-7 sentence, and the Hebrew primary preferred the complete 3:1-7 charge-verdict oracle.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Extending through 3:7 would erase the renewed direct-opposition formula and first-person exposure actions at 3:5.

rulings.rationale: The renewed speaker formula, first-person actions, public reaction, and abandonment questions create a clear oracle after the causal charge in 3:4.
rulings.counterevidence: This unit remains causally dependent on 3:1-4, and the Hebrew primary treated the whole 3:1-7 as one charge-verdict movement.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Merging 3:1-7 would preserve accusation and sentence together but hide the 3:5 speaker-and-form reset that makes the exposure oracle locally recoverable.

rulings.rationale: Example, narrated outcome, and direct inference are inseparable: the comparison cannot stand without the fall, and the verdict cannot stand without the comparison.
rulings.counterevidence: The direct second-person prediction at 3:11 is a local voice shift and 3:12 continues the same address.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Splitting 3:8-10 from 3:11 would detach the you-also application that states why the comparison was introduced.

rulings.rationale: Exposed defenses, frantic preparation, consuming consequence, multiplication, and disappearance form one cumulative futility taunt whose insect bridge begins in 3:15.
rulings.counterevidence: Nahum 3:16 changes the referents from siege preparation to merchants, guards, and officials; literary and canonical primaries favored that child seam.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Splitting 3:12-15 from 3:16-17 would distinguish fortress preparation from merchant and official imagery but interrupt the multiply-then-vanish locust reversal.

rulings.rationale: Leadership collapse, communal scattering, fatal injury, outside response, and closing question form the terminal royal lament-coda.
rulings.counterevidence: Verse 19 broadens from internal collapse to hearers' reaction while retaining the same second-person wound address.
rulings.rejected_alternative: Attaching 3:18-19 to 3:12-17 would keep institutional collapse together but conceal the explicit royal vocative and final lament form.
